title: Bamsi Beyrek
author: Anonymous (Book of Dede Korkut), adapted by Lantern

summaryTr: Beşikten nişanlı olduğu Banu Çiçek'le tam evlenecekken düşman baskınında kaybolan Beyrek'in yıllar süren macerası: tutsaklık, kaçış ve sevgiliye giden uzun yol. Dede Korkut Kitabı'nın en bilinen boylarından birinin B1 düzeyinde sade anlatımı.
paragraphs: ## A Promise in the Cradle
The old storyteller Dede Korkut used to tell this tale beside the camp fires of the Oghuz, a Turkish people of the wide plains. It begins at a great feast.

One spring the khan Bayındır, the ruler of all the Oghuz, put up his huge tent, and the beys, the lords of the tribe, came to sit with him. Among them was an old bey called Bay Büre. He looked at the khan's young son and at the sons of the other great beys. Suddenly he sighed, took out his handkerchief and began to cry out loud.
Kazan Bey, the strongest hero of the Oghuz, went down on his knees in front of him. "Bay Büre, why are you crying?"

"How can I not cry?" said the old man. "I have no son. One day I will die, and nobody will sit in my place or live in my tent. I want only one boy who will stand before the khan like these young men."

At once the beys raised their hands to the sky. "May God give you a son," they prayed. The prayers of the Oghuz beys were always answered. Then another bey, Bay Bican, stood up. "Pray for me too, my friends. I have no child. May God give me a daughter." The beys prayed again. "Be my witnesses," said Bay Bican. "If God gives me a daughter, she will be promised to Bay Büre's son. They will belong to each other from the cradle."

Some time later, both prayers were answered. A son was born to Bay Büre, and a daughter was born to Bay Bican. Bay Büre called his merchants. "Go to the land of Rum, far to the west, and buy the best gifts you can find for my son," he told them. In Istanbul they bought a grey horse with a coat as bright as the sea, a strong bow, and a heavy iron club with six sharp edges. These were gifts for a hero, and many years would pass before the merchants came home with them.
## The Boy Without a Name

The boy grew fast. At ten he could hit a bird in the air. At fifteen he was a tall, bold young man, and everybody liked him. But he had no name yet. The Oghuz had an old rule: a boy received his name only after he had fought an enemy and won.

One morning he rode out to hunt, and the hunt took him to his father's horse pasture. There he and his forty friends put up a striped tent and rested. Far away, something very different was happening.

At the Black Pass, a narrow road between two mountains, the merchants had stopped for the night. They were on their way home with Bay Büre's gifts. But the lord of a nearby castle, an enemy of the Oghuz and of their faith, had spies on every road. That night five hundred of his riders attacked the camp. They took all the goods and captured the older merchants. Only the youngest man escaped, and he ran, alone and out of breath, towards the Oghuz lands.

At the edge of the Oghuz land he saw a striped tent. A handsome young man sat in front of it with forty friends. The merchant had never seen him before, and he fell on his knees. "Brave young man, help me!" he cried. "Five hundred riders from the castle have taken our goods and my brother!"

The young man was holding a golden cup. He threw it on the ground. "Bring my horse and my armour!" he shouted. "Whoever loves me, follow me!" They found the enemy sitting in a circle, dividing the stolen money. The young man drew his sword and rode into them like a storm. Many of the enemy fell, and the rest ran away. Soon the goods were safe and the prisoners were free.

"You have done a hero's work," said the merchants. "Take anything you like from our goods." The young man chose three things: the grey horse, the bow and the iron club. The merchants went quiet. "Have I asked too much?" he said. "No," they answered, "but we brought these three things for the son of our bey, Bay Büre's boy, whom people call Bamsı." They did not know that they were talking to that boy.

The young man bit his finger. "It is better to receive my gifts from my father's hand," he thought, "than to take them here and owe a favour." So he said nothing, turned his horse and rode away. "What a fine young man!" said the merchants.

That evening Bay Büre heard that his merchants had come home, and he was delighted. He sat down in a great tent with his son on his right side. When the merchants came in, they bowed to the bey. Then they saw who was sitting at his right hand, and they hurried across the tent and kissed the young man's hand. Bay Büre grew angry. "What is this? I am sitting here, and you kiss my son's hand before mine?"

"Is he your son, my lord? Then please do not be angry. If he had not helped us, our goods would be lost, and we would all be prisoners in the enemy's castle." Bay Büre looked at his son. "So he has fought and won? Then it is time to give him a name."

Dede Korkut came, and he put his hand on the boy's head. "May God let you keep this son, Bay Büre. When he climbs the black mountains of snow, may God show him the pass. When he crosses a flooded river, may God show him the ford. When he rides into a crowd of enemies, may God give him his chance. His name will be Bamsı Beyrek, the rider of the grey horse. I have given him his name. May God give him a long life."
## The Girl in the Red Tent

Soon afterwards the beys went hunting, and Beyrek rode with them on his grey horse. He chased a deer far away from the others, over hills and across a wide meadow. At last he caught it. When he looked up, he saw a red tent in the grass.

He did not know whose tent it was. It belonged to Banu Çiçek, the daughter of Bay Bican, the girl who had been promised to him in the cradle. She had been watching him through the door. "Does this young man want to show off in front of us?" she asked her maids. "Go and ask him for a share of his deer."

An older woman went out to him. "I am no hunter," said Beyrek. "The whole deer is yours. But tell me, please, whose tent is this?" "It belongs to Banu Çiçek, the daughter of Bay Bican." Beyrek's heart began to beat fast. He bowed politely and rode away.
Banu Çiçek looked at the deer and thought for a moment. "I was promised to a boy I have never seen. Could this be him?" She put on a veil and called him back.

"Where do you come from?" she asked through her veil. "From the middle of the Oghuz lands. I am Bamsı Beyrek, the son of Bay Büre. Bay Bican has a daughter, and I came to see her." The girl raised her chin. "A man like you will never see her. But I am her closest friend, and I will find out what you are made of. If your horse is faster than mine, if your arrows are better than mine, and if you can throw me to the ground, then you may win her too." "Very well," said Beyrek. "Let us begin."

Beyrek's grey horse flew past hers. His arrow split her arrow in two. "Now let us wrestle," said the girl. They took hold of each other. First he tried to throw her, and then she tried to throw him. "If a girl beats me," thought Beyrek, "the Oghuz will laugh at me all my life." He found new strength, took her round her slim waist and laid her on her back on the grass.

"Young man," she said, "I am Banu Çiçek." Beyrek stared, and then he laughed. He kissed her three times and gave her one little bite. Then he took a gold ring from his finger and put it on hers. "Let this ring be a sign between us," he said. "Now go and ask for me properly," she answered.

Beyrek rode home. "Father, find me a wife," he said. "Find me a bride who is worth a long ride." Old Bay Büre smiled. "You want Bay Bican's daughter, Banu Çiçek. But she has a brother called Deli Karçar, and deli means mad. He kills every man who asks for her."
The beys chose Dede Korkut to go. "Give me two fast horses from the khan's stable," he said. "If he chases me, I will change horses on the way." He took the two horses and set off.

Banu Çiçek's brother, Deli Karçar, was sitting in front of his white tent. When he heard why the old man had come, he foamed at the mouth with anger. "Bring my black horse!" he shouted, and he rode after Dede Korkut. They crossed ten hills, until Dede's first horse was tired. Quickly he jumped on the second one, but Deli Karçar caught up with him and raised his sword. "If you strike me," cried Dede Korkut, "may your hand dry up!" At that moment the hand stayed in the air, and Karçar could not move it.
"Help me!" he cried. "In the name of God, I will give my sister to Beyrek!" Dede Korkut prayed, and the hand came down again, as strong as before.

"Now I want a bride price," said Deli Karçar. "Bring me a thousand horses that have never met a mare, and a thousand rams that have never met a sheep. Bring me a thousand dogs with no tails and no ears. And bring me a thousand mosquitoes too. If you cannot, I will kill you."

Bay Büre chose the horses and the rams from his own herds, and Dede Korkut found the dogs and the mosquitoes. How he did it, nobody knows. Deli Karçar was pleased with the horses and the rams, and he laughed when he saw the dogs. "But where are my mosquitoes, Dede?" "They live in one place," said Dede Korkut. "Come with me, and take off your fine clothes." He led Deli Karçar to a marsh and left him there. The mosquitoes covered him from head to foot. "Dede, help!" he cried. "Throw yourself into the water!" called Dede Korkut. Deli Karçar jumped into the river, and the water carried the mosquitoes away. After that he did not argue any more.
## The Wedding That Never Happened

Now the wedding could begin. In those days an Oghuz groom shot an arrow, and his wedding tent was put up where it fell. From the bride's family came a gift, a red coat. Beyrek put it on, but his forty friends did not look happy. "You wear red, and we wear white," they said. Beyrek laughed. "Today I will wear it, and tomorrow my deputy will wear it. Each of you will have a turn."

But a spy of the enemy had been watching them. He rode to the lord of Bayburt castle. "Bay Bican has given his daughter to Beyrek, and tonight he enters the bridal tent!" The lord gathered seven hundred riders and set off at once.

In the night the enemy burst into the tent. Beyrek's deputy drew his sword. "My head for Beyrek's head!" he shouted. He fought bravely, and he fell. The enemy caught Beyrek and thirty-nine of his friends, tied their hands and carried them away to Bayburt castle.

At dawn Bay Büre came to the wedding tent. It was empty and torn. He threw himself down and tore his clothes. "My son! My son!" he cried. Beyrek's mother wept, and his seven sisters put on black clothes. Banu Çiçek put on black too. "My beloved," she cried, "why did you leave me alone?"

Sixteen years passed. Nobody knew if Beyrek was alive or dead. Then Deli Karçar went to the khan's court. "If Beyrek were alive, he would have come home. I will give a bag of gold for news that he is alive. And I will give my sister to the man who brings news that he is dead."

A man named Yaltacuk, the son of Yalancı, stood up. In Turkish yalancı means "liar", and the son was just like his father. "I will go," he said. Long ago, Beyrek had given him a shirt that Banu Çiçek herself had sewn. Now he put blood on it and brought it back to the khan. "They killed Beyrek at the Black Pass," he said. "Here is the sign."

The beys cried. Bayındır Khan said, "Take it to his bride. She sewed it, so she will know it." Banu Çiçek knew it at once, and she cried until she could cry no more. So Yaltacuk held the small wedding feast, and the day of the great wedding was fixed. Banu Çiçek could not go against her brother's word.
## Sixteen Years Behind Castle Walls

Bay Büre never stopped looking for his son, and he sent his merchants out once more. "Bring me news of Beyrek, alive or dead." The merchants rode day and night, and at last they came to Bayburt castle. By chance it was a feast day, and the lord had ordered his prisoner to play the kopuz, an old stringed instrument, for his guests.

From a high place Beyrek saw the faces of the merchants, and he knew them at once. He called to them in a song and asked about his father and mother, and about Banu Çiçek. The merchants sang back: "Your parents are crying for you. Your sisters wear black. And your bride has been promised to Yaltacuk, who told the Oghuz that you were dead. Fly out of Bayburt like a bird, Beyrek! Come to your own wedding, or Banu Çiçek will be lost to you for ever."

Beyrek sat down among his friends and cried. The lord's young daughter came to see him, as she did every day. She had grown fond of him. "Why are you so sad?" she asked. "For sixteen years I have been your father's prisoner," said Beyrek. "I had a bride, and now she is going to marry another man."

The girl thought for a long time. "If I let you down the castle wall on a rope, and you reach your family safely, will you come back here and take me away with you to your people?" Beyrek gave his oath. "If I reach home safely and do not come back for you, may my own sword cut me down."

The girl brought a rope and let him down the wall. Beyrek stood on the ground and thanked God. He walked towards the castle's pastures, hoping to find a horse. There, eating grass, was his own grey horse, which the enemy had taken from him. The horse saw him and knew him. It stood on its back legs and neighed. Beyrek put his arms around its neck and kissed its eyes. "You are my brother, better than a brother," he said, and he jumped on its back.

He did not ride away at once. At the castle gate he shouted to the guards, "My thirty-nine friends are in your hands! If one of them is missing, I will kill ten of you in his place!" Forty riders rushed after him, but they could not catch the grey horse.

On the road to the Oghuz lands, Beyrek met a minstrel, a travelling singer with a kopuz. "Where are you going?" "To a wedding," said the minstrel. "Yaltacuk is marrying the bride of Bamsı Beyrek." "Give me your kopuz," said Beyrek, "and take my horse. Look after it for me. I will come back, pay you for the kopuz, and take my horse again." The minstrel looked at the beautiful horse and agreed at once.

Near his father's camp he met some shepherds piling up stones beside the road. "Why are you piling them up?" asked Beyrek. "A liar brought news of our young bey's death and is marrying his bride," they said. "He will pass this way, and we will throw these stones at him." "May your faces always be white," said Beyrek. In the old Oghuz way of speaking, a white face meant honour.

At last he came to the big tree at his parents' camp. His youngest sister had come to fill her jug at the spring under it. She was crying. "My brother Beyrek, my brother Beyrek! Since you went away, our feasts are black." Beyrek could hardly hold back his tears. He sang to her, and she sang back, "Singer, all these mountains and cold waters were my brother Beyrek's. Since he went away, nobody rides these horses. Go to the wedding, singer. There they will give you food."

He went on to his older sisters, who were sitting in black clothes. "I am hungry," he said. "Have you got some bread for me? And an old coat of your lost brother's, to wear to the wedding?" They fed him and brought him one of Beyrek's coats. It fitted him perfectly, and his eldest sister looked at him with wet eyes. "If your eyes were not so sunken," she said, "and if your hair did not cover your face, I would say, 'Brother Beyrek.'"

Beyrek said to himself, "My sisters almost know me. The beys may know me too. But first I want to see who my friends are among the Oghuz, and who my enemies are." He gave the coat back and found an old camel-hair sack, made a hole in it and pulled it over his head. Then he walked towards the wedding like a man who had lost his mind.
## The Stranger at the Wedding

At the wedding the beys were shooting arrows. The khan's son Budak shot, and everybody shouted, "May your hand be safe!" But when the bridegroom Yaltacuk took his turn, nobody cheered. "May your hand dry up," some of them muttered. Yaltacuk saw the strange man in the camel sack and shouted, "Hey, you madman! Pull my bow, or I will cut your neck."
Beyrek took the bow and pulled it. The bow broke in two. "It is only good for shooting sparrows," he said. "Bring Beyrek's old bow!" said Yaltacuk. "Let us see what this madman can do with it."

They brought the bow, and Beyrek knew it at once. It was the strong bow the merchants had bought for him in Istanbul. He thought of his friends in the prison, and he nearly cried. "Beys," he said, "for the love of you I will shoot." The target was the bridegroom's ring, and Beyrek's arrow hit it and broke it into pieces. The beys clapped their hands and laughed with joy.

Kazan Bey had been watching, and he called the strange minstrel to him. "What do you want, mad minstrel? A rich tent? Gold?" "My lord, I only want to eat." "Let him have his way," said Kazan to the beys. "Today he is the bey." Beyrek ate until he was full. Then he kicked over the big cooking pots, and the food ran in every direction. Kazan only laughed.

Then Beyrek went to the tent where the women sat. He chased away the drummers and the pipers and sat down in the doorway. "I want the bride to get up and dance while I play the kopuz," he said. Two women stood up first, but Beyrek's songs made them so angry that they sat down again. Then Kazan's wife, Burla Hatun, said to the bride, "Girl, get up and dance. What else can you do?"

Banu Çiçek put on her red coat and pulled the long sleeves over her hands. She danced, and Beyrek played and sang a song that made fun of her and of the whole wedding. She grew angry. "Am I a shameful woman," she cried, "that you say such things to me?" She pushed back her sleeve, and her white wrist showed. On her finger was a gold ring.

Beyrek saw the ring, and his heart jumped. He sang, "Since Beyrek went away, girl, did you tear your black hair? Did you cry from your black eyes? The gold ring on your finger is mine. Give it to me, girl." She answered in a song, "I have torn my hair, and I have cried a thousand tears. But you are not Bamsı Beyrek, whom I loved. This ring is not yours. Many gold rings look alike. If you want it, tell me its sign."

Beyrek sang, "Girl, did I not bring a deer to your tent on my grey horse? Did my horse not beat yours, and my arrow split yours? Did I not throw you to the ground, kiss you three times, bite you once, and put a gold ring on your finger? Am I not Bamsı Beyrek, whom you loved?"

Then Banu Çiçek knew him. She threw herself at his feet, and the women brought a coat and dressed him as a bey again. Then she jumped on a horse and rode as fast as she could to bring the news to his parents. "Your son Beyrek has come home after sixteen years!" she sang. "What will you give me for good news?" "If it is true," said Beyrek's father, "then everything I have is yours."

Then the beys brought Beyrek. But the old man's eyes had gone blind from crying for sixteen years. "I must be sure," he said. "Let him cut his little finger and rub the blood on my eyes with a handkerchief. If I can see again, he is Beyrek." Beyrek did it. When the handkerchief touched his father's eyes, they opened by the power of God. His mother saw again too. They fell at their son's feet and cried and thanked God.

Yaltacuk heard the news, and he ran away in fear. He hid in a bed of reeds. Beyrek went after him and set the reeds alight. Yaltacuk ran out, knelt under Beyrek's sword and begged for his life. Beyrek forgave him.

"Not until I have freed my friends will I rest," said Beyrek. "Whoever loves me, get on your horse!" cried Kazan Bey. The Oghuz heroes rode to Bayburt. The fight in front of the castle was short and fierce, and the Oghuz won. Beyrek found his thirty-nine friends alive and well. He had not forgotten the lord's daughter, who had let him down the wall. He kept his oath: he took her out of the castle and brought her safely to the Oghuz camp, where nobody touched her.

Then they all went back to the white tent, and this time the wedding began for real. Forty tents rose on the grass, and the feast lasted forty days and forty nights. At last Beyrek and Banu Çiçek, who had waited for sixteen years, were married.

Then Dede Korkut came, took his kopuz, and sang the tale from the beginning. "May your black mountains never fall," he said. "May your shady tree never be cut down. May God never part a son from his brother. May God forgive your sins, and may everyone who says amen see the face of God."

glossary.bay: bay (Türkçe unvan; Bay Büre, Bay Bican kişi adlarında)

quiz.q: Why does Bay Büre cry at the khan's feast?
options: His best horse has died
He has no son
He is afraid of the khan
He is too old to ride
quiz.explainTr: Bay Büre'nin oğlu yoktur; öldüğünde yerini ve çadırını kimsenin almayacağını düşünüp ağlar.

quiz.q: What does the young man choose from the merchants' goods?
options: Gold and silk
A red tent and a veil
A grey horse, a bow and an iron club
Forty swords
quiz.explainTr: Boz atı, yayı ve gürzü seçer; ama bunlar aslında kendi babasının tüccarlarının ona götürdüğü hediyelerdir.

quiz.q: How does Banu Çiçek test Beyrek in the red tent?
options: She races him, shoots arrows with him and wrestles him
She asks him to bring a thousand horses
She makes him answer difficult riddles
She sends him to fight her brother
quiz.explainTr: Banu Çiçek peçesini takıp kendini 'en yakın arkadaşı' diye tanıtır; Beyrek'le at yarışır, ok atar ve güreşir.

quiz.q: How does Beyrek escape from Bayburt castle?
options: He digs a tunnel under the wall
Kazan Bey's army breaks the gate
The merchants pay money for him
The lord's daughter lets him down the wall on a rope
quiz.explainTr: Kale beyinin kızı Beyrek'e gönül verir; geri dönüp kendisiyle evleneceğine söz alınca onu ip yardımıyla surdan indirir.

quiz.q: How does Banu Çiçek finally know that the stranger is Beyrek?
options: His old coat fits him perfectly
Dede Korkut tells her the truth
He sings about the red tent and the gold ring he gave her
His horse neighs outside the tent
quiz.explainTr: Beyrek, kırmızı çadırdaki karşılaşmayı ve parmağına taktığı altın yüzüğü şarkıyla anlatınca Banu Çiçek onu tanır.
